'''James Stephen Brooks''' (July 18, 1944 – September 27, 2014) was an American physicist who specialized in experimental physics at high magnetic fields and cryogenic temperatures. He was a professor at [[Florida State University]] and director of the Condensed Matter Experimental Group at the [[National High Magnetic Field Laboratory]].

== Biography ==
Brooks was born in [[Chicago, Illinois]], on July 18, 1944, and was raised in [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]], where the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] is located. His father was a chemical engineer who participated in the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name="PT">{{cite journal|last1=Naughton|first1=Michael J.|last2=Boebinger|first2=Greg|last3=Hallock|first3=Robert|title=James S. Brooks|journal=[[Physics Today]]|date=January 8, 2015|doi=10.1063/PT.5.6121}}</ref><ref name="HC">{{cite web|title=James Brooks Obituary|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/houstonchronicle/name/james-brooks-obituary?id=7886777|publisher=Houston Chronicle|date=October 2, 2014|accessdate=October 2, 2026}}</ref>

He graduated from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1966, and earned his PhD from the [[University of Oregon]] under the supervision of [[Russell J. Donnelly]] in 1973.<ref name="PT"/>

He was a postdoctoral researcher at the [[University of Minnesota]] and then at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]]. In 1979, he took up a position as an assistant professor at [[Boston University]], being promoted to professor in 1991. In 1994, he moved to [[Florida State University]], where he was the Grace and William Moulton Professor of Physics and Chair of the Department of Physics. He also served as a director of the Condensed Matter Experimental Group at the [[National High Magnetic Field Laboratory]] until his death.<ref name="PT"/>

In 1999, he was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] for his "experiments measuring magneto-transport properties in organic conductors".<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellows Archive, Search recipients: james sbrooks|url= https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship?q=james%20sbrooks&af=true |accessdate=October 2, 2026}}</ref>

He died on September 27, 2014, at his home in [[Alligator Point, Florida]].<ref name="PT"/><ref name="HC"/><ref name="DB">{{cite web|title= In Memoriam: Jim Brooks|url=https://nationalmaglab.org/about-the-maglab/organization/history/in-memoriam/jim-brooks/|author=David Barfield|publisher=National High Magnetic Field Laboratory|accessdate=October 2, 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==
Brooks specialized in experimental physics at high magnetic fields and cryogenic temperatures. He enabled studies in this field by constructing experimental environments combining high-field resistive magnets and [[dilution refrigerator|dilution refrigerators]], which he used to conduct research on [[superfluidity]], [[heavy fermion material]]s, [[organic conductor]]s, and [[organic superconductors]].<ref name="DB"/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Brooks|first=James S.|title= Organic crystals: properties, devices, functionalization and bridges to bio-molecules|journal=Chem. Soc. Rev.|year=2010|volume=39|issue= 7|pages=2667–2694|doi= 10.1039/b913417b}}</ref>
